entities.summary: Mikołaj Kurowski of Szreniawa of Kurów was a chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland and a Catholic hierarch. He held the posts of the bishop of Poznań, bishop of Włocławek and an archbishop of Gniezno. Releasing the name or adoptive Mirosław.

entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mikołaj Kurowski (c. 1355 – September 16, 1411) emerged as a towering ecclesiastical and political figure in the late 14th and early 15th-century Kingdom of Poland, serving as a pivotal advisor to King Władysław II Jagiełło. His career trajectory, spanning from the bishopric of Poznań to the archbishopric of Gniezno – the primate see of Poland – cemented his influence over both the spiritual and temporal affairs of the burgeoning Jagiellonian state. Kurowski's ascent coincided with a critical period of Polish expansion and consolidation, marked by the Union of Krewo and the ongoing geopolitical struggle with the Teutonic Knights, placing him at the heart of strategic decision-making.

Beginning his ecclesiastical career, Kurowski was consecrated Bishop of Poznań in 1395, a crucial administrative center. His political acumen quickly became evident, leading to his appointment as Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland in 1402, a post he held concurrently with the powerful Bishopric of Włocławek from 1399. The zenith of his power came in 1403 when he was elevated to Archbishop of Gniezno, making him Primate of Poland. In this capacity, Kurowski played a significant role in Polish diplomacy, particularly in mediating disputes with the Teutonic Order and strengthening the Jagiellonian dynasty's position through ecclesiastical appointments and statecraft. He was instrumental in preparing Poland for the impending conflict with the Order, advising King Jagiełło on both military and diplomatic fronts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mikołaj Kurowski was a pivotal figure in the early Jagiellonian Kingdom of Poland, serving as Chancellor and Archbishop of Gniezno. His strategic counsel significantly contributed to Poland's political stability and military preparations against the Teutonic Order, directly influencing the outcome of the Battle of Grunwald.
